power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.05", Text = "Bold pvalues indicate statistical significance (p < 0.05 after class-wise FDR adjustment)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.292", Sentence = "OR 1.80, p = 0.292), and atypical dissociation, associated with benignity only in the AI model (OR 0.07, p = 0.007)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 46 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: The requirement for informed patient consent was waived in accordance with Section 29 of the Saxon Hospital Act (SächsKHG) for retrospective analysis of routinely collected clinical data.
No identifiable individual patient data or identifiable photographs are included in this study.
We evaluated a framework combining foundation-model-based whole-slide analysis with AIpredicted morphological features and manual PRAME status.

Although overall diagnostic performance was comparable to the standalone model, integrating these criteria as statistically significant predictors aligns the algorithmic output with established histopathological parameters.
This study demonstrates the feasibility of combining computational models with standard histopathological workflows.
Correlating algorithmic predictions with established criteria facilitates potential clinical applications, including automated case triaging and diagnostic decision support.
Diagnosing melanoma, a type of skin cancer, under a microscope can be challenging.
In difficult cases, doctors may sometimes reach different conclusions.

Artificial intelligence (AI) computer programs can accurately analyze digitized tissue samples, but they often function as "black boxes," making it difficult for doctors to understand how the AI reached its conclusion.
In this study, we tested an AI system on 1,000 skin samples.

Instead of relying solely on the AI to provide a final diagnosis, we combined its analysis with specific microscopic features that doctors routinely look for, alongside the results of a special laboratory test called PRAME.
We found that the AI system was highly accurate in identifying melanoma.

While combining the AI with the specific tissue features and the PRAME test did not further increase the overall accuracy, it successfully aligned the computer's output with established medical standards.
This approach demonstrates that advanced computer models can be integrated with traditional laboratory tests.

By linking AI results to familiar medical criteria, the system's output becomes more transparent for physicians, which could help doctors evaluate difficult skin tissue samples more efficiently in the future.
Malignant melanoma represents one of the most aggressive and lethal forms of skin cancer 1,2   .

While histopathological examination remains the established gold standard for diagnosis and staging 1, 3, 4 , the microscopic evaluation of melanocytic lesions is inherently subjective, relying on cellular atypia, architectural asymmetry, and pagetoid spread.

text.text: For AI to be safely adopted in routine dermatopathology, clinical interpretability is essential 25, 26 .

text.text: One approach is to assess whether learned image representations can predict established histopathological criteria, such as dermal mitoses, ulceration, or junctional atypia, alongside the primary malignancy classifier 27 .

text.text: Recent studies confirmed that deep learning models reliably assess such histological structures with accuracies exceeding 92% 28 , bridging machine learning and human evaluation to support human-in-the-loop workflows 11, 27.

text.text: While deep learning can infer molecular alterations directly from standard H&E slides if distinct morphological correlates exist 29 , automated digital quantification of dedicated immunohistochemical stains, such as PRAME (Preferentially Expressed Antigen in Melanoma), substantially reduces interobserver discordance compared with manual scoring 30   .

text.text: In challenging melanocytic lesions, PRAME has emerged as a sensitive and specific diagnostic tool 31 .
text.formatted: In challenging melanocytic lesions, PRAME has emerged as a sensitive and specific diagnostic tool <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> .

text.text: However, the reliability of inferring PRAME expression from routine morphology remains uncertain in borderline lesions.
Integrating PRAME as an independent input therefore provides non-redundant information that complements automated image analysis and improves model robustness across cohorts 32, 33.
text.formatted: Integrating PRAME as an independent input therefore provides non-redundant information that complements automated image analysis and improves model robustness across cohorts <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref>.

text.text: The objective of this study was to evaluate a diagnostic framework combining foundationmodel-based WSI analysis with manually assessed PRAME immunohistochemistry in melanocytic lesions.

We first assessed the diagnostic performance of a slide-level malignancy classifier and evaluated whether foundation-model representations could predict established histopathological criteria and immunohistochemical markers.
We subsequently examined the performance of an integrated model combining the slide-level malignancy score, AI-predicted morphological features, and manually assessed PRAME status.
The study design, digitization, computational workflow, and evaluation strategy are illustrated in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The study design, digitization, computational workflow, and evaluation strategy are illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: This retrospective, single-center study at the Department of Dermatology, University Hospital Carl Gustav Carus, TU Dresden, identified all melanocytic lesions with PRAME immunohistochemistry selectively requested for diagnostically challenging cases between January 1, 2020, and January 21, 2025.

From 1,360 consecutive cases, nonmelanocytic lesions, re-excision specimens, mucosal or uveal melanomas, and metastases were excluded to restrict the dataset to primary cutaneous melanocytic neoplasms.

All corresponding hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), PRAME, and routine immunohistochemical slides (SOX10, MelanA, HMB45, Ki-67), were digitized using an Aperio AT2 scanner (Leica Biosystems, Wetzlar, Germany) at 40x magnification.
text.formatted: All corresponding hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), PRAME, and routine immunohistochemical slides (SOX10, MelanA, HMB45, Ki-67), were digitized using an Aperio AT2 scanner (Leica Biosystems, Wetzlar, Germany) at 40x magnification.

text.text: The final cohort comprised 1,000 H&E WSIs from primary cutaneous melanocytic lesions.
text.formatted: The final cohort comprised 1,000 H&E WSIs from primary cutaneous melanocytic lesions.

text.text: Multiple distinct lesions were excised in 87 patients, and multiple sections were digitized for 44 specimens.
Each digitized section was treated as an independent slide-level observation.
Patient age, sex, diagnostic category, PRAME status, and all 18 histological criteria were documented for all 1,000 WSIs, anatomical location in 988 cases, and Ki-67 expression in 316 stained WSIs.
Due to fragmented historical reporting, conventional melanoma subtypes and chronic sun damage were not included.

In 19 WSIs exhibiting exclusively junctional features despite an original report documenting a dermal component on other section levels, the slide-level diagnostic ground truth was adjusted from invasive melanoma to melanoma in situ to align with the digitized section, leaving binary malignancy unaffected.
The reference diagnosis was established from original histopathology reports issued by boardcertified dermatopathologists.
All malignant diagnoses (melanoma in situ and invasive melanoma) underwent mandatory institutional second-opinion review, with borderline cases resolved by interdisciplinary consensus.
A single investigator, blinded to the reference diagnosis, systematically evaluated the 18 histological criteria, PRAME scores, and Ki-67 proliferation index.
While all 18 criteria were utilized for baseline characterization (Table 1) and feature concordance (Supp.
text.formatted: While all 18 criteria were utilized for baseline characterization (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>) and feature concordance (Supp.

text.text: Tables S1, S3), a curated core set of 13 tumor-specific features was selected for machine-learning benchmarking and multivariable integration, excluding nonspecific infiltrates (dense infiltrates, TILs), anatomical compartments (junctional/dermal components), and subcutis infiltration.
text.formatted: Tables <ref type="table">S1</ref>, <ref type="table">S3</ref>), a curated core set of 13 tumor-specific features was selected for machine-learning benchmarking and multivariable integration, excluding nonspecific infiltrates (dense infiltrates, TILs), anatomical compartments (junctional/dermal components), and subcutis infiltration.

text.text: Standardized definitions for each morphological feature and scoring protocols for PRAME and Ki-67 are documented in the Supplementary Criteria Catalog (Supp.
Material S2).
Blinded to clinical history, the investigator recorded regression strictly as horizontal fibrosis and neovascularization.
Computational analysis used the open-source STAMP framework.
Digitized WSIs underwent automated tissue segmentation to exclude background, and tissue regions were divided into non-overlapping tiles of 224×224 pixels (256×256 µm; 1.14 µm/pixel).
Feature embeddings were extracted using the Virchow2 foundation model, mapping each tile to a 2,560-dimensional vector.

Slide-level aggregation used an attention-based transformer model to train separate classifiers for binary malignancy, all 18 morphological criteria, and multiclass immunohistochemical markers (PRAME and Ki-67), evaluated via a one-versus-rest (OvR) approach.
Complete hyperparameter specifications are provided in the GitHub repository.
The dataset was partitioned chronologically, allocating the earliest 80% of cases (n=800) to the training set and the most recent 20% (n=200) to an independent test set.
To prevent data leakage, allocation was performed at the patient level, assigning all lesions and sections from a single patient to the same partition.
Model optimization used 5-fold cross-validation within the training cohort on NVIDIA CUDA-enabled GPUs, with final evaluation on the independent test set.
Statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.3; tidyverse, pROC, PRROC, broom).
Baseline comparisons used the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for continuous variables and Pearson's chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables.

Model performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC; 95% CIs via DeLong's method) and precision-recall curve (AUPRC), applying an OvR approach for multiclass endpoints.
Continuous AI probability scores for histological features were calibrated on the training cohort using logistic regression to establish operational decision thresholds.
Concordance between calibrated AI predictions and the expert reference standard was evaluated using confusion matrices.

To evaluate predictor associations and compare diagnostic modalities, logistic regression models were fitted across three stages: the standalone slide-level AI malignancy model, a multivariable morphology model based on the 13 core features, and a multivariable logistic integration framework ('Triple Model') combining the slide-level AI malignancy score, the 13 AI-derived morphological probabilities, and the clinical PRAME score (0-4).
Predictor associations were quantified as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs and p-values, including a prespecified contrast comparing PRAME score 4 versus 0.
All tests were two-sided (p<0.05).

text.text: Applying a chronological rather than random train-test split introduced natural temporal domain shifts in tissue processing, scanner calibration, and disease prevalence, closely reflecting prospective deployment.

Despite compositional differences, particularly a higher proportion of melanoma in situ in the test set, diagnostic performance remained stable, indicating that extracted representations capture invariant morphological features rather than temporal laboratory artifacts.
The slide-level malignancy classifier demonstrated high standalone accuracy.

While testcohort performance slightly exceeded internal cross-validation, this difference likely reflects cohort composition and sampling variability rather than systematic shifts in diagnostic practice.
Clinically, by maintaining complete precision up to a substantial recall threshold, the classifier identified two-thirds of malignant lesions without false-positive diagnoses in the test cohort.

In routine pathology, this profile could support automated triage, prioritizing high-confidence cases before expert review, although prospective validation with predefined operating thresholds remains required to confirm clinical utility.
This performance in borderline melanocytic proliferations marks a clear advance over earlygeneration machine learning approaches.

Whereas multi-center meta-analyses of task-specific CNNs reported pooled concordance indices around 0.87 34 , large-scale foundation models such as Virchow2 20 utilize self-supervised pre-training across millions of WSIs to overcome representational bottlenecks and enable clinical-grade decision support.

text.text: Evaluating the 13 histological criteria confirmed that foundation model representations support predicting established histopathological features 28 .
text.formatted: Evaluating the 13 histological criteria confirmed that foundation model representations support predicting established histopathological features <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> .

text.text: Structural criteria such as ulceration, dermal mitoses, and ordered single cells were predicted with high accuracy, reflecting dermatopathological domain knowledge.

In contrast, discrete cytomorphological criteria proved more challenging to resolve, reflecting the difficulty of capturing high-power nuclear details spanning few pixels within tile embeddings, where localized signals are diluted during slide-level attention pooling.
In multivariable regression, models driven by automated feature predictions achieved diagnostic performance comparable to expert human annotations.

Beyond classification accuracy, translating continuous slide embeddings into discrete histological criteria aligns deep-learning representations with conventional pathological reasoning, establishing a transparent foundation for human-in-the-loop workflows [24] [25] [26] [27] 35.

text.text: A performance drop emerged when predicting immunohistochemical status directly from standard H&E morphology, with classifiers for PRAME expression or Ki-67 proliferation performing substantially worse than morphological predictors.
text.formatted: A performance drop emerged when predicting immunohistochemical status directly from standard H&E morphology, with classifiers for PRAME expression or Ki-67 proliferation performing substantially worse than morphological predictors.

text.text: While computational models can predict specific molecular alterations from routine histology across cancers 29 , PRAME expression in diagnostically challenging melanocytic lesions cannot be reliably predicted from H&E alone.
text.formatted: While computational models can predict specific molecular alterations from routine histology across cancers <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> , PRAME expression in diagnostically challenging melanocytic lesions cannot be reliably predicted from H&E alone.

text.text: In this borderline setting, targeted immunohistochemistry provides non-redundant biological information not fully encoded within standard histological patterns.

Because immunohistochemical status cannot be reliably inferred from routine histology alone, the Triple Model integrated clinical PRAME scoring with AI-predicted morphological features and the slide-level malignancy classifier, preserving high predictive performance comparable to the standalone classifier.

Within this multivariable framework, clinical PRAME status emerged as a strongly associated independent predictor alongside automated predictions of junctional atypia, dermal atypia, and the slide-level classifier.
Thus, automated morphology and immunohistochemistry provide complementary, non-redundant diagnostic value.

While proof-of-concept studies explored digital PRAME quantification in small cohorts 30 , our study demonstrates across 1,000 lesions that integrating this biomarker directly with an H&E foundation model provides a practical framework for clinical decision support.
text.formatted: While proof-of-concept studies explored digital PRAME quantification in small cohorts <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> , our study demonstrates across 1,000 lesions that integrating this biomarker directly with an H&E foundation model provides a practical framework for clinical decision support.

text.text: The Triple Model highlights that the greatest utility of computational dermatopathology lies in combining physical biomarkers with automated morphological analysis rather than predicting immunohistochemistry purely from H&E 32, 33.
text.formatted: The Triple Model highlights that the greatest utility of computational dermatopathology lies in combining physical biomarkers with automated morphological analysis rather than predicting immunohistochemistry purely from H&E <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref>.

text.text: This study has several limitations.

First, while chronological splitting provides rigorous temporal validation, the retrospective single-center design necessitates external validation across diverse scanning hardware and independent cohorts.
Second, annotation by a single pathologist ensures high internal consistency but does not capture inter-observer variability, underscoring the need for multi-reader validation.

Third, the integrated Triple Model did not substantially improve discrimination over the standalone slide-level classifier, indicating that the incremental clinical benefit of model integration requires prospective evaluation.
Finally, restricting the cohort to cases with clinically requested PRAME staining introduces selection bias.
Thus, our findings reflect a pre-filtered, challenging diagnostic spectrum rather than unselected routine biopsies.
This study demonstrates that histopathology foundation models achieve robust diagnostic discrimination in identifying malignant melanoma within clinically challenging, borderline lesions.
Automated profiling of discrete histological criteria translates continuous image embeddings into transparent features aligned with human expertise.
However, key molecular biomarkers cannot be replaced by routine morphology alone.

By uniting standard H&E features with clinical PRAME scoring, the integrated Triple Model combines high diagnostic accuracy with interpretability for computer-assisted decision support in dermatopathology.

text.text: During the preparation of this manuscript, the authors utilized Gemini (Google) as an editorial and computational assistant.

Specifically, the tool was employed to expand author-generated notes and bulleted drafts into continuous prose, refine syntax, condense text to meet journal constraints, and assist in drafting and optimizing R, Bash, and Python scripts utilized for data processing and statistical workflows.
All scientific concepts, study designs, analytical pipelines, and data interpretations originated entirely from the authors.

Following AI-assisted drafting and script generation, the authors rigorously reviewed, tested, verified, and refined all code and textual content to ensure complete computational reproducibility, factual integrity, and scientific accuracy.
The authors take full responsibility for the final text, data analyses, and overall integrity of the published work.

To control for type I error accumulation, multiple testing adjustments were performed using the Benjamini-Hochberg (False Discovery Rate, FDR) procedure, applied strictly and independently within each individual class of hypotheses (the nevus subclassification family, the melanoma in situ subclassification family, and the group of 18 morphological criteria, respectively).

'Corrected Diagnosis (Slide-level)' refers to a retrospective histopathological re-evaluation of the specific slide used for AI analysis, noting that in some cases only in situ components were present despite a caselevel diagnosis of invasive melanoma.

Subclassification percentages for nevi, melanomas in situ, and invasive parameters are calculated relative to their respective main diagnostic categories and may exceed 100% due to overlapping clinicopathological features.
